problem: The 10° retarded curve lies above the MBT curve at low speed: at 1000 rpm retarded gives 24.04 % while 'MBT timing' gives only 21.04 %. The curves cross near 1350 rpm. MBT timing is defined in Section 2 as the timing that gives the highest brake torque (and hence best efficiency) at a given speed and mixture, so a retarded curve can never be above it anywhere. A student reading the graph will learn the opposite of the definition.
fix: Redraw so the 10° retarded curve stays below the MBT curve at every speed, still peaking earlier and lower (for example: MBT 30 − 3.5×10⁻⁶(x−2600)², retarded 28 − 4.0×10⁻⁶(x−2300)², which peaks near 2300 rpm at 28 % and stays under MBT over the whole 1000–5000 rpm range).

problem: 'Cold coolant and cold oil raise friction and poor fuel vaporisation' is grammatically broken and a student may read 'raise ... poor fuel vaporisation' as raising a quantity rather than worsening it.
fix: 'Cold coolant and cold oil raise friction and make fuel vaporisation poorer, so BSFC rises.'

problem: 'Brake thermal efficiency is the inverse idea' is vague; it does not say what is inversely related to what.
fix: 'Brake thermal efficiency is the reciprocal idea: η_bth = 1 / (BSFC × LCV), so the speed of minimum BSFC is also the speed of maximum brake thermal efficiency.'

where: Section 2, lean mixture and best efficiency
problem: The reason given for the lean best-efficiency point, 'because there is less fuel for the same work', is circular and does not match the standard explanation.
fix: 'Best brake thermal efficiency comes from a slightly lean mixture, φ around 0.85 to 0.95, because combustion is more complete, the throttle is more open (lower pumping loss) and no extra fuel is supplied beyond what the air can burn.'

problem: 'Engine ratings exist so that these effects are separated from weather and test-cell conditions' is unclear — ratings do not remove the effects, they state the reference conditions.
fix: 'Engine ratings are quoted at agreed reference air conditions so that a result measured on a hot day or in a different test cell can be compared with the maker's figure.'
